title: Stock market falls for a second week, banks lead the way down
excerpt: High oil prices, jitters about US government debt, and a sell-off in the big four banks all pushed the share market lower this week.
body:
The Australian share market, called the ASX, closed lower for the second week in a row. The drop was driven by high oil prices, jitters about US government debt, and a sharp sell-off in the big four banks: Commonwealth Bank, Westpac, ANZ, and NAB.

Our take: the bank sell-off is the more interesting part of this story. The big four are now trading at 18 to 20 times next year's expected earnings, down from 22 to 24 times a year ago. That means investors are willing to pay less for each dollar of bank profit. The reason is that banks are not making as much money from the gap between what they charge on loans and what they pay on deposits. Deposits, the money in your savings account, are catching up to loan rates after years of being much lower, and that is squeezing the banks' profit margins.

The dividend payouts, the cash payments banks send to shareholders out of their profits, are creeping up to 4 to 4.5 per cent on the share price, which is starting to look attractive again for people who want income from their investments. The big question is whether this is a buying opportunity or the start of a long decline. We think it is the former: the banks' balance sheets, the money they have in reserve, are stronger than they were during the 2008 financial crisis, and the banking regulator APRA's rule that caps dividend payouts at 4.5 per cent of assets is still in place, which means dividends should hold even if profits fall further.

The high oil price is a near-term worry for inflation. If the oil price stays above $90 a barrel for another month, the Reserve Bank is more likely to push back the timing of the next interest rate cut.

Our take, in plain terms: if you already own bank shares, do not panic. If you have been thinking about buying, the dividend yield is now interesting. If you are wondering what to do about your mortgage, nothing changes this week, variable rates are still not expected to fall until late 2026 at the earliest.
whatItMeans: If you own bank shares: Watch the dividend payouts, the cash you receive. At 4 to 4.5 per cent, the big four are starting to look attractive again, but only if you can handle another 10 per cent drop from here without selling in a panic.

If you have money in a high-interest savings account: Expect the rates to start falling within six months. Banks are losing their best growth channel as their share prices fall, and they will look for cost savings, including paying less on deposits.

If you have a mortgage: Variable rates, the rate that moves up and down with the Reserve Bank, are unlikely to fall until late 2026 at the earliest. The bank share-price weakness is about their profit margins, not about loan defaults.
If you drive a car: The oil price spike will pass through to petrol prices within four to six weeks. Budget an extra $10 to $15 per tank if it holds.
